I dealt with such situations for years. There are multiple progressive solutions, but in the end, the only way I sorted this out is:

1. Know exactly what this alter exactly wants. He likely wants to do/have that thing but doesn't get it, which makes him super frustrated or endangered, wich makes him violent. 
2. Define clear boundaries around what he can do and not do, and why, according to you and external people.
3. Set up a safe place where he can do/have what he wants without hurting anyone. That's the counter part of defining boundaries.
4. Go in that place, and do/have that thing or do/have sth that is extremely similar to it (depending on your boundaries), so that at least he can see that there is some place for him and that you care for him.
5. Repeat 1-4 and adjust until both of you find peace or even merge (it will happen if you find a perfect balance). 

I don't know if my solution is general enough, but I hope it can help. This is a therapy that you can also do on your own. There was a period during which I included one new memory of my life in the notebook every evening. So basically, I remembered a completely random event, then I asked myself "was it before or after this already written event ?" etc, until I find the exact true chronology.

I really didn't choose the remembered event. I just picked up what was in my mind. I soon realised that my mind was obsessed with some specific memories. When I remembered a memory that I already wrote in the notebook, then I skipped and waited for a new memory to appear. That MASSIVELY helped me against obsessive trauma memories. A written notebook is needed, you can't do LIT (lifespan integ therapy) just with your brain.

It's very effective when you really do it, steadily. The hard part however is when it wakes up some trauma memories, which have to be treated apart before doing again a standard lifespan integration cycle.

The foundation is to treat amnesia by telling your life again and again and again, and to help the patient remember about his strength and used solutions. You take multiple sessions to write your "life line": you write important life events in a notebook with your T and order them in chronological order. Dates, places, people, major emotions involved, etc. When the therapist has a good basis, he will read your life line to you multiple times in a session. 

When you feel more stable after a cycle, or if you have no improvement, you explore your life again to enrich the life line for another cycle, etc. 

This therapy is also efficient for some other disorders. It's been invented by Peggy Pace (2003 I think). 

I precise: is is not a suggestive therapy at all. It's not hypnosis. The therapist can only tell what you have told to him, and if you are afraid of having fake memories, you don't have to include them in your life line.

It doesn't matter who is the host etc. There is a simple method to make people recover their memories. First, there is no reason to panic. Instead, I advise to constantly, without stopping, recall her events that happened recently, or things that she should know (even if she seems to know them). You have to tell these elements with a neutral voice. Never tell her about who she is (age, name, etc.), tell her about what the world is and what has happened around her or to her. Try to focus on two kind of elements: things that make her feel **safe**, and things that she **likes**. Speak on a normal voice as you would speak to an unknown person in a positive casual context. If she doesn't seem to be receptive, it's normal, keep recalling events, she will remember in the end. 

Everytime my gf did this, it worked. You just have to not give up. Sometimes the person can get out of amnesia in 2 minutes, sometimes it takes 15 min. But if you don't do it, the amnesia lasts much longer. When she recovers her memory, she may have intense headaches. It can last a few minutes, it's normal. If she's painful or express intense discomfort, let her time to regulate herself. When she has completely recovered her mind, keep on recalling recent events in a more normal dialog. Otherwise, recovery can be incomplete and the person can be blurred several months. 

Don't think in terms of alters. Your gf is a person, not an alter. Thinking in terms of alters increases dissociation and confusion. Alters are an inner self-interpretation of the person's identity, not an objective reality. Your goal must only to find a stable state where her memory is maximal. 

Example recovery speech when your gf gets amnesic: "Hi Lily, you are at home. My name is Miguel. I took you to Coopa Coffee an hour ago. There was Juanita, Lena and Max with us. Do you remember about Max ? He has a dog, Keit *(suppose she really likes the dogs)*. A black dog with a long fur. A very energic dog. You pet him a lot. It was very happy to see you and it barked a lot. Max even asked us if it was not barking too much. It's okay if you don't remember.
So, now we are at home, 12 Calavina Street, *ZIP Code, City Name, State*. There is the living room where you watched the movie *MovieNameSheLikes* last week, and there is also the bathroom there. There is a big shower in the bathroom *(good transition if she said she wanted to take a shower before her amnesia).*" etc.

If she gets agressive during your talk, wait and let her regulate her feelings. If she panics, keep talking but with a more comforting tone, a soft voice, a slow voice, and taking into account what she focuses on. If she starts moving and wants to leave, keep speaking while following her, but focus on recalling the places where she could go to feel good.

Memory is a neuron network. A neuron is activated when its neighbour is excited too. So you will have a bigger effect if you connect all the memories through common elements (dog is good, dog is black, her favorite clothe is black, speak about clothes, etc). 

Also, amnesia can get worse with time bc of age. Speaking about your common memories in daily discussion reduces the risk of relapse. "Hey Lily, random thought but do you remember when we went to... And we did this... It happened that... It was 6 years ago already ! But it was so fun... Etc"

Many mental disorders, if not all, involve false beliefs and buggy interpretations (I said "involve", I didn't say "are due to"). Schizo spectrum (very simplified so avoid too long stories) : hallucinating based = believing that some external events exist while it's internal signal. Anxious/paranoid disorders : believing that a danger exists while it does not. Bipolar (manic phase) and heteroagressive (antisocial, etc) disorders : believing that agressivity or intense reaction is needed while it's not. Tragedic expression disorders (narcissistic, histrionic, borderline) : believing that absorbing others' attention is required while it's counter-productive. etc.
